summary: This informational memo argues that IETF documents tend to be written for implementers, so reviewers are overwhelmed by details. It encourages writing a protocol model that shows the essential design and makes review easier.

plainLanguage.summary: Internet standards are checked by volunteers with little spare time, and most specifications are written for the people who will build them rather than for reviewers. This memo asks authors to add a short overview so that reviewers can see the shape of a protocol before reading the details.

subtitle: A short guide to the overview document that lets reviewers grasp a protocol before wading into its details.

tldr.problem: IETF documents are written for implementors, so the volunteers who review them are overwhelmed by detail, which leads to long review times and poor reviews.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends a short protocol model that answers three questions: what problem is being solved, what messages flow and what they mean, and what important but unobvious features exist. It is best shown with a few simple diagrams.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines no protocol. It gives guidance, illustrated with models of STUN, DCCP, WebDAV COPY and MOVE, and IKE.

today: RFC 4101 is an Informational memo from the IAB, published in June 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It gives guidance rather than a standard: it defines no protocol and, in its own words, has no security issues.

sections.title: Why IETF Documents Are Hard to Review
sections.content:
The IETF process depends on peer review, but the documents submitted for publication are often extremely difficult to review. Reviewers have only limited time, which leads to very long review times, poor reviews, or both. A large part of the problem, in the author's view, is that most documents never present an architectural model of how the protocol operates. They describe the protocol and leave the reviewer to work it out.

That is acceptable when a document is written for implementors, because they need to understand the protocol in full anyway. It is much harder work for reviewers. They need the big picture first, so that they can identify the important or difficult parts and focus their attention there. They simply do not have time to give the whole document the attention an implementor would.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet standards are checked by volunteers with little spare time. Most specifications are written for the people who will build them, so reviewers get swamped in detail. This memo asks authors to add a short overview so reviewers can see the shape of the protocol first.

sections.title: The Three Questions a Model Answers
sections.content:
A protocol model has to answer three questions. What problem is the protocol trying to achieve? What messages are being transmitted and what do they mean? And what are the important, but unobvious, features of the protocol?

The idea is to give a reader enough information that they could design a protocol roughly like the one being described, sharing its most important features. Choosing a key distribution centre model for authentication, as Kerberos does, is such an essential feature. Choosing ASN.1 rather than S-expressions, or XML had it existed at the time, is only an implementation decision, and either would have served equally well.

The purpose of a model is explicitly not to give a complete or alternative description of the protocol. It is a big-picture overview, so that readers can quickly understand the essential elements of how the protocol works.
sections.plainLanguage: A model has to answer three questions: what problem is being solved, what messages go back and forth, and which parts of the design are important but not obvious. It is not a shorter version of the specification.

sections.title: Principles for Writing a Model
sections.content:
Three principles guide the presentation. Less is more: people can only hold a very small number of pieces of information in their head at once, so a lot of detail has to be dispensed with. The simpler the model, the better. Abstraction is good: abstracting pieces away is a key technique for representing complex systems, the way a map is better than a photograph for finding out where you want to go. Authors should not be afraid to compress several protocol elements into one abstract piece for the sake of explaining them.

The converse of the second principle is that a few well-chosen details sometimes help. Many people work better with examples, so it is often good to describe the material in the abstract and then give one concrete piece to bring the description into focus. Authors should focus on the normal path, and discuss error cases and corner cases only where they help to make an important point.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep it short, use abstraction to hide unimportant detail, and add one concrete example when that helps. Leave out error cases unless they teach something important.

sections.title: The Three-Part Structure of a Model
sections.content:
Models are easiest to grasp in visual form, so the recommended format centres on a few key diagrams with explanatory text for each. The diagrams should be simple and typically consist of boxes and arrows: boxes for the major components, arrows for their relationships, and labels for important features. The presentation is structured in three parts, one for each of the questions above, and each part should hold one to three diagrams.

The first part describes the problem. It starts with a short statement of the environments the protocol is expected to be used in, describes the relevant entities and the likely scenarios in which they take part, and includes a diagram of the major communicating parties and their relationships. It is particularly important to lay out the trust relationships between the parties, because those are often unobvious. The example given is STUN, a protocol that lets a machine behind a network address translation gateway work out its own external address, drawn as a SIP client, a NAT gateway and a STUN server exchanging a question and an answer.

The second part gives a broad overview of the protocol, showing in ladder diagram or boxes-and-arrows form the messages that flow between the agents, with explanatory text describing the purpose of each message and the major data elements. It should not contain detailed descriptions of the messages or the data elements: no bit diagrams, no ASN.1 modules and no XML schema. Its purpose is to give a map that shows where each detailed piece fits. A state machine of the network elements' behaviour may be included, but kept as minimal as possible. The example is DCCP, which is datagram-oriented like UDP but stateful like TCP, and whose connections pass through four phases: initiation, feature negotiation, data transfer and termination.

The third part covers important protocol features that are not obvious from the message flow, such as high-level security considerations, congestion control information, or an overview of the algorithm the network elements follow. Authors should think carefully before writing it: if there is nothing important to say, they should leave it out. The example is WebDAV, where MOVE is not the same as COPY followed by DELETE, because the copy would temporarily exceed a quota, would need permission to create files that the user may not have, and would give the new file a different creation date. One practical obstacle runs through all of this: RFCs have to render as ASCII, so authors may find it easier to produce a separate model in Postscript or PDF and make it available at review time, though an archival version would be handy.
sections.plainLanguage: A model is presented as three parts with a few simple diagrams: the problem and who trusts whom, the messages that flow, and anything important that the message flow does not show.

sections.title: A Complete Example: IKE and Its Environment
sections.content:
The memo's complete worked example is the Internet Key Exchange (IKE), described as one of the most complicated security protocols ever designed by the IETF. IKE is a key establishment and parameter negotiation protocol for Internet protocols, and its primary application is establishing security associations for IPsec authentication headers and encapsulating security payloads. The IPsec engines and the IKE engines are typically separate modules. When no security association exists for a packet that needs to be processed, the IPsec engine asks the IKE engine to establish one; the IKE engine contacts the peer and, once the handshake is finished, registers the association with the IPsec engine. Traffic between the peers can also be used to refresh keying material or adjust operating parameters such as algorithms.

The environment section sets out the properties a reader needs before the messages make sense. IKE is not symmetrical, unlike IPsec: the party that sends the first message is the initiator and the other is the responder. The design also had to provide perfect forward secrecy, so that traffic stays protected even if the long-term keying material is later compromised and the session-specific material is gone; denial of service resistance, because IKE lets arbitrary peers start computationally expensive cryptographic operations; and keying assumptions, since both sides must in general be authenticated and IKE supports a flexible model of shared keys, digital signatures or encryption keys. The working group also wanted some identity protection, so that peers can hide their identity from passive observers, and the designers chose to make the party that speaks first identify first.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example is IKE, the protocol that sets up IPsec keys. The model first explains where IKE sits in the stack and what it has to achieve, such as forward secrecy and resistance to denial of service, before describing any message.

sections.title: The IKE Handshakes
sections.content:
At a high level there are two kinds of IKE handshake: ones that establish an IKE security association, and ones that establish an authentication header or encapsulating security payload association. Two peers that have never spoken before must first establish an IKE association, which lets them exchange an arbitrary amount of protected IKE traffic and then run a second handshake for the AH and ESP associations. The memo calls the first stage Stage 1 and the second Stage 2, to avoid the confusing mix of phases and modes in IKE's own wording, and notes that there can be more than one Stage 2 handshake once Stage 1 is finished.

Stage 1 handshakes fall into two categories. Main Mode is a six message, three round trip handshake that provides identity protection and denial of service resistance. In the first round trip the initiator offers a set of algorithms and parameters, and the responder picks one set and returns it along with a cookie. In the second round trip the initiator sends its Diffie-Hellman public share and echoes the cookie, and the responder returns its own share, so that both can compute the shared key, though neither yet knows that the connection has not been attacked. As long as fresh shares are generated for each handshake, forward secrecy is provided. The cookie exchange is the basic defence against denial of service: it forces the peer to show that it can receive traffic, which foils blind attacks such as SYN floods and lets the responder check the cookie before doing the expensive key agreement. In the final round trip the peers prove their identities inside the encrypted channel. At the end of Main Mode they share a set of algorithms for encrypting further IKE traffic, traffic encryption and authentication keys, and mutual knowledge of the peer's identity.

Aggressive Mode packs more data into fewer messages to reduce latency, but it gives no identity protection and no denial of service protection, because the authentication data is sent in the clear and the responder does the key agreement without waiting for a round trip.

Stage 2, which IKE calls Quick Mode, is where the associations that protect other traffic are established. The first two messages set the algorithms and parameters, including the transforms to apply and the kinds of traffic to protect, and the final message is a check over the previous ones. The peers derive fresh keying material from the Stage 1 keying material, using nonces for freshness, and Quick Mode can also carry a new Diffie-Hellman handshake for per-traffic forward secrecy. The memo closes with points that deserve special attention, such as how cookies are generated: the verification must not need a list of valid cookies, because an attacker could otherwise consume memory by repeatedly asking for them. The recommended way is a single master key and a hash of the secret and the initiator's address information.
sections.plainLanguage: IKE runs in two stages. Stage 1 sets up a protected channel between the peers, either in the careful six-message Main Mode or the faster Aggressive Mode. Stage 2 uses that channel to agree the keys for the traffic that will actually be protected.
